chunk_findings.detail:
The change teaches the config validator's user-facing error text that the new watchdog section is called `health`, but the change's own specification defines every watchdog knob under a `[watch]` section — `[watch].stall_s`, `[watch].idle_s`, `[watch].reply_s`, `[watch].crash_s`, `[watch].interval_s`, `[watch].act` — and the CONFORMANCE clause requires "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt". The known-sections list in these two lines contains `... gates, health, ids, ...` and no `watch` anywhere (alphabetically it would sit between `upgrade` and `worktree`). Demonstrated input: an operator who follows the documented keys writes

    [watch]
    stall_s = 300
    act = "advise"

and ddflow rejects it with exactly the message these transcript lines encode — "unknown config section [watch]. Known sections: agent, bugs, …, health, …, worktree" — so the watchdog's limits/modes are not settable under the names the spec defines, and the "everything configurable" requirement is not met for this feature. Either the section must be exposed as `watch` (and this golden string must list it) or the spec's knob names must be reconciled; a test transcript whose expectation was edited to match "health" makes the mismatch self-consistent rather than fixing it.

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the top-level guard `if mode not in HW.MODES: return O.failed(...)` with a check over the *effective per-kind* modes (`bad = sorted({m for m in by_kind.values() if m not in HW.MODES})`). Because `HW.modes(cfg, mode)` is what fills `by_kind` (and the surrounding code shows it does no validation of its own — otherwise the new `bad` check would be unnecessary), the caller-supplied `mode` override is only reachable through kinds whose config is `"inherit"`. If every `[health].mode_<kind>` knob is set explicitly (e.g. `health.mode_stalled="apply"`, `health.mode_idle="apply"`, `health.mode_unresponsive="apply"`, `health.mode_locked="apply"`, `health.mode_crashed="apply"`, `health.mode_runaway="apply"`), then `by_kind` is entirely built from config, `bad` is empty, and an invalid mode passes through untouched: `ddflow health inspect --mode bogus` (also reachable via the MCP/prompt surfaces) no longer fails with `unknown mode 'bogus'`. Execution then continues with `mode` still `"bogus"`, so the outcome reports `mode:"bogus"` and `HW.record_run(log, "bogus", ...)` writes the watchdog run event with a mode value that is not one of `HW.MODES`, while the actual corrections were driven by the per-kind values. The previous code rejected this input unconditionally; validating `by_kind` instead of the resolved `mode` (or validating both) is needed to keep the guard.

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the single global gate (`cfg.health.mode == "off"`) with `all(m == "off" for m in HW.modes(cfg).values())`, i.e. the function now runs whenever *at least one* finding kind is not off. That is only correct if the findings themselves are filtered by their kind's mode somewhere, and nothing in this change does that: the only mode-aware logic added here is the short-circuit, and the `found = [...]` list that follows is produced unconditionally from `cycles`/`activity`. So with the documented per-kind knob in its own docstring (`"off" inspects nothing in the periodic pass`): set `[health] mode_idle = "off"` while the other kinds keep their `propose` default, and `all(m == "off" ...)` is False, so `health_lines` no longer returns `[]` and idle/unresponsive/locked lines for the kind the operator switched off are still emitted (and, if the same resolved mode map drives the ladder, still acted on) whenever any other kind is enabled. The input that demonstrates it is an operator config that turns off exactly one kind (`mode_locked = "off"` or `mode_idle = "off"` with the rest at the default `propose`): the gate at line 53 evaluates to False and health output for the disabled kind is produced, contradicting the contract the same diff writes into `HealthConfig.mode` ("`off` inspects nothing in the periodic pass", "mode_idle, mode_stalled, ... override it for one kind"). A per-kind-aware pass needs the per-finding kind check (skip f when `HW.modes(cfg)[f.kind] == "off"`), not just an all-off early exit.

chunk_findings.detail: The added block defines a per-finding-kind mode for six of the seven finding kinds the change is specified around: idle, stalled, unresponsive, locked, crashed, runaway — but not for STARVED. The intent enumerates STARVED as a first-class finding kind ("STARVED = context or quota pressure from the governor (P-governor sampling) so the lane cannot continue ... every found condition is a finding with evidence") and requires the correction ladder to be configurable "as a ladder with a mode per step ([watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise, per finding kind)", with the conformance requirement that "every limit, mode and interval a knob ... per project and org". Concretely: an operator whose governor starts flagging starved lanes sets `[health].mode_starved = "off"` (or `"propose"`) to handle that kind independently; no such knob is registered, so the per-kind setting cannot resolve and the generic `[health].mode` continues to govern starved findings along with everything else — exactly the coupling the per-kind knobs exist to break. The other six kinds each get their own knob, so this is an omission in the new block rather than a deliberate grouping.

chunk_findings.detail: `_unresponsive` decides UNRESPONSIVE purely from `now - lane.asked_at`, yet the condition it implements (and the text it emits, "asked … ago, no progress and no release since") requires knowing the lane produced **no progress after the ask**. The helper is handed only `lane`, `waiters` and `now` — no progress watermark (or any other "the ask was answered" signal) — so it cannot separate a lane that ignored the nudge from one that answered it by resuming work while keeping its lease. Concretely: lane L is nudged at T (because it was idle); L commits at T+5s and keeps working; at `now = T + reply_s` the watchdog calls `_unresponsive(L, [], now)`, gets `age = reply_s`, and reports "no progress and no release since" — a false statement. In `act` mode that finding feeds the ladder (the fix string itself says `park {lane.holder}'s lane`), so the watchdog parks a lane that is actively producing work, which breaks the stated invariant "never acts on a lane with progress" / "never discards work". If the intent is that `inspect()` only calls this helper for lanes whose watermark is still `<= asked_at`, that check has to exist somewhere and is not derivable from the data this function receives; as written the "no progress since" claim is unverified. (Secondary: `asked_at` is documented "0.0 for none", and `now - 0.0` gives a ~1.7e9-second age rather than "no ask", so any call for a never-nudged lane yields "asked 56 years ago" instead of being suppressed.)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new "dead process" branch is gated on `ln.work is not False`, and it `return`s unconditionally once the outer condition holds:

```python
if ln.live and ln.gone and limits.crash_s > 0 and now - ln.renewed_at >= limits.crash_s:
    if ln.work is not False:
        out.append(_dead(ln, now))
    return
```

Per the intent, `CRASHED = the holder's process or session is gone ..., or its lease expired with work attached` — the work qualifier applies only to the expired-lease clause, not to the gone-process clause (that clause exists precisely so "a dead process is seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL"). Concrete input: lane with `live=True` (lease still within TTL, `now - renewed_at = 120`), `gone=True` (pid definitely exited), `work=False`, `limits.crash_s=60`, `limits.stall_s=300`. The outer condition is true, `ln.work is not False` is false, so nothing is appended and the function returns. Because of the early `return`, the lane is also not eligible for STALLED/IDLE/UNRESPONSIVE, and the bottom CRASHED check (`if not ln.live ...`) is skipped since `ln.live` is true — the watchdog emits **no finding at all** for a lane whose process is definitively dead. The dead holder keeps its lease until the TTL lapses (the exact "stopped agent found by hand" case the change is meant to remove), and any lane waiting on that lease stays blocked; the ladder never gets a finding for the holder, so it can never park/relaunch it. This mirrors a real reachable state: a lane whose process died after/without any recorded work item (e.g. a subagent whose work field is empty).

chunk_findings.detail:
The record files are read with `f.read_text()` and only `OSError` is caught:

```python
try:
    name = f.read_text().strip()
except OSError:
    continue
```

`Path.read_text()` decodes with the locale/UTF-8 codec, and a decoding failure raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, which is a `ValueError`, not an `OSError`, so it is not caught. The identity directory is shared state written by other processes; if a record file contains bytes that are not valid UTF-8 (e.g. a non-ASCII agent name whose write was truncated by a killed harness process, leaving an incomplete multibyte sequence), `read_text()` raises, the exception escapes `liveness`, and `inspect()` — the watchdog's per-call crash check — raises instead of reporting a finding. The crash detector then fails on every call until the bad file is removed, defeating the feature; a `errors="replace"`/`errors="ignore"` read or catching `UnicodeDecodeError` would keep it read-only and total.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/harness_identity.py:liveness

chunk_findings.detail: `asked` is produced by `steps_of(...)`, which converts the stored cadence record with `clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")` — i.e. it is a timestamp on the same (injectable / simulated) clock the spec's regression tests use ("Regression tests with fake lanes and a fake clock"). `stop_notice` then computes the elapsed time with `time.time()`, the raw wall clock, instead of the same clock that produced the record. Under the fake clock required by the spec the two are unrelated: a stop recorded "5 s ago" on the fake clock at T yields `asked == T-5`, while `time.time()` returns the real epoch R (≈1.7e9), so the age handed to `clock.fmt_age` is `R-(T-5)` and the holder is told the watchdog asked it to stop decades ago (or, if the fake clock runs ahead of wall time, a negative age). Any test that asserts the notice text, and any real invocation whose clock is simulated, gets a bogus age even though `steps_of` correctly found the stop record. The elapsed-time computation needs to come from the same `clock` abstraction (e.g. `clock.now() - asked`) that generated the record.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/healthwatch.py (stop_notice, the `clock.fmt_age(time.time() - asked)` line)

chunk_findings.detail:
The refactor gates STALLED (and UNRESPONSIVE) correction on `f.evidence["waiters"]`, which the old `_break` did not do (it consulted `WT.waiting_for(st, cfg, f.item, now)` directly).

- In `_stalled_move`, `if not f.evidence.get("waiters"): return None` means a STALLED finding whose evidence carries no waiters produces *no move at all* — not even the ladder's first rung (nudge/stop). Given a lane that stalls while holding a renewed lease and that no other lane is currently waiting on (exactly the operator's 2026-10-15 case: an agent idle for an hour with a live lease, and the intent's `STALLED = no progress for [watch].stall_s while its lease is renewed`), `correct(..., findings=[STALLED(item="L1", evidence={...})], mode={"stalled": "apply"})` iterates the finding, `_stalled_move` hits line `if not f.evidence.get("waiters"): return None`, and returns `[]` — no nudge, no stop, no park, so the watchdog's core purpose is not served.
- The handoff is also a dead end: when a stop *was* requested and `now - asked >= cfg.health.reply_s`, `_stalled_move` returns `None` with the comment "the UNRESPONSIVE finding takes it from here", but the only UNRESPONSIVE handler in `correct` is `elif f.kind == H.UNRESPONSIVE and f.evidence.get("waiters"):`. UNRESPONSIVE is defined as "a nudge or yield request went unanswered" (evidence about the outstanding request, not about a wait-for edge), so if that finding's evidence has no `waiters` key the branch is skipped and the blocked, stalled lane is never parked/broken (its lease keeps being renewed) — the ladder silently halts after the stop request, contradicting the intent's requirement that the ladder escalates step by step (nudge → … → park → take over/relaunch) for STALLED/UNRESPONSIVE.

The `waiters` key is only needed by `_park_break` (which already re-derives claimants via `WT.waiting_for` and returns `None` if there are none); gating the earlier rungs and the UNRESPONSIVE kind on it turns several findings into no-ops.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/healthwatch.py:_stalled_move / correct (H.UNRESPONSIVE branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes the direct `h.mode == "off"` guard and replaces it with `all(m == "off" for m in modes(ctx.cfg).values())`. If `modes()` enumerates the per-kind `mode_<kind>` overrides (which is the shape its name and the newly advertised `mode_<kind>` knobs suggest) rather than resolving every kind against the global `[health].mode`, then with the default config — `[health] mode = "propose"` (or `"apply"`) and no `mode_<kind>` keys set — `modes(ctx.cfg)` is the empty mapping, `all(...)` over an empty iterable is vacuously `True`, and `cadence()` returns `[]`. The periodic watchdog pass is then never due even though the operator has the feature enabled, so no lane can ever be detected. The guard must retain the global mode, e.g. only suppress when `h.mode == "off"` *and* every explicit override is `"off"`. The input that demonstrates it is a repo with a single live lease and `[health] mode = "propose"`, `interval_s = 60`, no `mode_*` entries: the pass reads as not-due forever.

chunk_findings.detail: The watchdog spec enumerates the finding kinds as STALLED, IDLE-HEARTBEAT, LOCKED, CRASHED, RUNAWAY, UNRESPONSIVE and STARVED, and requires "a mode per step … per finding kind" with "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt" (r-everything-configurable). This diff adds a `mode_*` knob for every one of those kinds except STARVED: `mode_crashed`, `mode_idle`, `mode_locked`, `mode_runaway`, `mode_stalled`, `mode_unresponsive` are present, and the alphabetical sequence `stalled` → `unresponsive` leaves exactly the slot where `mode_starved` would sit. The remaining `mode_*` entries all carry the identical `inherit`/`health.mode` boilerplate, so the omission is not a deliberate different treatment — as written, a starved-lane finding (governor context/quota pressure, P-governor.sampling) has no per-kind mode to read: `health.mode_starved` resolves to nothing, so an operator cannot set it to `off`, nor override the inherited `health.mode` for that kind as they can for the other six. If the knob exists in another slice of this change this finding is moot; within the change as presented it is absent.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff drops the `mode` property from the `ddflow_health` input schema while leaving `"additionalProperties": false`. The intent for this change explicitly specifies that the correction ladder carries "a mode per step ([watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise, per finding kind)" and that the CONFORMANCE clause (r-everything-configurable) requires that "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt, per project and org". After this change an MCP client that previously issued `ddflow_health` with `{"run": true, "mode": "apply"}` (the old schema advertised `mode` = "off, propose or apply") is now rejected outright, because `mode` is no longer a declared property and `additionalProperties` is `false`. So the per-call mode override is no longer reachable over MCP even though the tool still advertises "run=true corrects per [health].mode and the mode_<kind> overrides" — the MCP surface has silently lost one of the configuration knobs the change's own conformance requirement says must be settable from every surface. If the intent was that mode is now only settable through project config, that needs to be deliberate (and MCP/CLI/prompt parity verified), not achieved by deleting the parameter from the schema.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten `health.stall_s` help text is internally contradictory and, taken literally, describes a progress rule that would suppress the very STALLED findings the watchdog exists for. It says a lane counts as showing progress if there was "a change in its worktree since the lease began", and then, in the same paragraph, says "neither is a file that was changed once and never again" progress. Those two statements cannot both hold: a file changed once after the lease began *is* a change "since the lease began" (so, per the parenthetical, it is progress and the lane is never STALLED), while the closing sentence says exactly that case is *not* progress. Concrete input: a lane takes a lease at T, writes one file at T+300s and then does nothing but renew its heartbeat; at T+stall_s (default 3600s) the parenthetical ("change since the lease began") marks it as progressing, so it is never reported STALLED — which is precisely the 2026-10-15 failure mode ("an agent sat idle for an hour with a current lease (a heartbeat loop kept renewing it)") the watchdog is supposed to catch. Only the closing sentence (a one-off change is not progress) yields the intended behaviour, so the parenthetical must be scoped to the current stall window (a change since the last inspection / since the progress watermark), not "since the lease began". As written, the operator-facing help documents a rule under which a stalled lane with any historical worktree write is never flagged.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr (health.stall_s description)

chunk_findings.detail: The recorded intent for this watchdog fixes the mode vocabulary: "mode off|advise|act" (with default advise), and the governing note that renames the CLI (`ddflow watch …` → `ddflow health …`) explicitly says only the CLI name changes — "The ladder stays: nudge -> ask status -> request yield -> park -> take over/relaunch -> escalate, mode off|advise|act." The help text added here instead advertises the per-kind knobs as taking `'off'`, `'propose'` or `'apply'` (e.g. `health.mode_idle`, `health.mode_stalled`, `health.mode_unresponsive`, `health.mode_locked`, `health.mode_crashed`, `health.mode_runaway`), i.e. a different vocabulary from the one the operator/roadmap specified. Concrete failure: an operator who follows the documented ladder and sets `health.mode = act` (or per-kind `health.mode_stalled = act`) hits the "unrecognised value" path described in the very same help text — a warning plus a silent fall back to `'propose'` — so the watchdog stays in report-only mode and never performs the stop/park/relaunch steps the operator asked for, with no error surfaced beyond a warning.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr:1681 (health.mode_idle / health.mode_stalled / …)

chunk_findings.detail: The old test ran the watchdog twice in `--mode propose` and asserted that the two findings lists were element-wise identical and that `(kind, item, holder)` keys were unique; the new test only runs one propose pass and checks `len(keys) == len(set(keys))` for that single pass. Findings are recomputed on every pass, so the requirement that findings are not duplicated/accumulated *across passes* is now untested: an implementation that persists findings and re-appends them (or otherwise returns pass-1 findings plus new ones on pass 2) would still satisfy `keys == set(keys)` on the single `first` pass, would still write exactly one `health_stop:T1` if the request dedup is based on the pending reply window rather than on the finding list, and would still return one non-applied "waiting" move on the 4th apply — so the new test passes while the removed one failed. Since the stated regression set explicitly requires "findings are deduplicated and rate-limited", dropping the only cross-pass check for this is a coverage regression in the change's own test file.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_health_watch.py (replacement of `test_findings_are_not_repeated_across_passes`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test encodes a CRASHED definition that is narrower than the one the watchdog is specified to implement. The intent defines CRASHED as "the holder's process or session is gone (lease heartbeats carry pid, host and session id so a dead process is seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL), **or** its lease expired with work attached". The "with work attached" qualifier attaches only to the *expired-lease* branch; the dead-process branch has no work condition. The test, however, builds `clean = H.Lane("T1", A, True, NOW - 30, work=False, renewed_at=NOW - 90, gone=True)` — a leader whose lease is still live (renewed 90 s ago, 30‑minute TTL not reached) and whose process/session is gone (`gone=True`) — and asserts `H.inspect([clean], [], [], [], NOW, LIM2) == []`, i.e. that no finding is produced because there is "nothing to lose". Given that input the spec requires a CRASHED finding within `crash_s` (60 s here, and `renewed_at` is already 90 s stale). As written, a dead lease holder with a clean worktree is silently ignored until the lease TTL lapses — up to 30 minutes — even though it still holds the task/lease and its dispatcher slot, which is exactly the failure mode ("seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL") the feature exists to prevent. The sibling integration test `test_a_dead_harness_...` only exercises the `work=True`/file-written case, so nothing else in this diff catches the gated behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_health_watch.py::test_a_live_lease_whose_process_is_gone_is_crashed_within_crash_s (the `clean` assertion)

chunk_findings.detail: The `declare` carve-out is keyed on the bare *enclosing function name* and is applied to **all six** `WATCHDOG` modules and to **every** `_deletes()` call inside that function, not just the identity-record write the comment names. Demonstration: add to `services/healthwatch.py` a method `def declare(self, lane): shutil.rmtree(lane.worktree)` (or `os.remove(lease_path)`, `lane_tree.rename(...)`). `_calls()` reports `fn == "declare"`, so the guard at line 98 evaluates `fn != "declare"` as False and skips the call; `test_the_watchdog_modules_signal_nothing_and_delete_nothing` passes while the watchdog has just destroyed a lane's work. This directly contradicts the module docstring's stated invariant that "The watchdog's own modules additionally may not delete anything at all," and the hole is not even scoped to `surfaces/declared/health.py` — any of the six listed modules may host a `declare` function and thereby gain an undetected delete/move/replace.

chunk_findings.detail: Detection keys on the literal call name (`f.attr` / `getattr(f, "id", "")`), so a trivially aliased import evades both `test_every_process_signal_in_ddflow_is_on_a_child_it_started` and the watchdog check. Input: `from os import killpg as _kp` followed by `_kp(pgid, signal.SIGKILL)` yields `name == "_kp"`, which is not in `KILLERS` and not handled by `_is_probe`, so no `unlisted`/`bad` entry is produced; likewise `getattr(os, "kill")(pid, signal.SIGKILL)` yields `name == "getattr"`. The docstring's claim that "every call that can end a process ... must be one of the sites below" is therefore unenforced against exactly the kind of accidental kill (signalling a pid ddflow did not start) the file exists to forbid.

chunk_findings.detail: The watchdog ladder the change is implementing is recorded as `[watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise` (intent §3), and the ROADMAP note only rebrands the CLI verbs (`ddflow watch inspect|…` → `ddflow health inspect|…`) — it does not rename the ladder knob or change its mode set/default. The transcript the change adds, however, fixes the watchdog's correcting mode as `health.mode = 'propose'` and then makes every per-kind setting (`health.mode_idle/stalled/locked/crashed/runaway/unresponsive = 'inherit'`) resolve to it. `'propose'` is not a member of the recorded `off | advise | act` set, and `advise` — the documented default — does not appear anywhere in the new block. Concretely: an operator who reads the documented ladder and runs with the documented default (mode `advise`, i.e. "write findings only, change nothing") gets the `propose` mode instead, and a config validated against the recorded enum (`off|advise|act`) would reject the fixture's default outright. If the intent is that `advise` was renamed, the golden transcript should record the recorded value; if not, the fixture enshrines a mode that violates the ladder contract.

chunk_findings.detail: Intent §1 enumerates seven findings that the watchdog must produce: STALLED, IDLE-HEARTBEAT, LOCKED, CRASHED, RUNAWAY, UNRESPONSIVE and STARVED (governor context/quota pressure, P-governor sampling), and §3 says the correcting mode is set "per finding kind" with the CONFORMANCE clause `r-everything-configurable` requiring every mode to be a knob. The new block supplies per-kind mode knobs for exactly six kinds (`mode_idle`, `mode_stalled`, `mode_unresponsive`, `mode_locked`, `mode_crashed`, `mode_runaway`) and none for STARVED. Given a lane that is STARVED by governor quota pressure, no per-kind mode can be set for it (it can only fall back to the base `health.mode`), so the per-finding-kind configurability the spec demands is absent for one of the enumerated kinds — and the golden transcript locks that gap in.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `[health].mode` doc states that `apply` "adds the auto-order `needs` edges that end a lease deadlock (this mode decides for the pass, whatever `[schedule].auto_order` says)", while the `schedule.auto_order` knob documented in this same surface says of `off`: "does nothing", and promises ddflow "never touches a done, abandoned or decide item, an item tagged no-auto-order, or adds an edge that would close a needs cycle". Two knobs therefore govern the same action and one silently overrides the other's explicit `off`. Input that demonstrates it: `[schedule] auto_order = "off"` (operator has switched off silent auto-rewiring) together with `[health] mode = "apply"`; a three-lane crossing-glob deadlock arrives, and the watchdog adds the `needs` edges anyway — the one action `auto_order = "off"` says will never happen. Nothing in the `health.mode` text commits the watchdog to the other two guards either, so an item tagged `no-auto-order` can be rewired, and an edge that closes a `needs` cycle can be added, after which the default `schedule.cycle_policy = "error"` refuses to schedule the queue at all. Either `auto_order`'s "does nothing" contract or the "whatever `[schedule].auto_order` says" override is wrong as written.

chunk_findings.detail: The governing note for this change fixes the watchdog's mode vocabulary as `off | advise | act` ("The ladder stays: nudge -> ask status -> request yield -> park -> take over/relaunch -> escalate, mode off|advise|act"), but the config text this diff commits documents `health.mode = 'propose'` and accepts only `'off'`, `'propose'`, `'apply'` (`health.mode_idle/stalled/unresponsive/locked/crashed/runaway` likewise). Concretely, an operator following the recorded vocabulary sets `ddflow config --set health.mode act` (or `advise`) to turn the correction ladder on; `act` is not a recognised value, so per the very text committed here the knob is "warned about, reported by `doctor` and falls back to 'propose'" — i.e. report-only. The watchdog then nudges nothing, parks nothing and breaks no lease, so the stall the change exists to correct (the 2026-10-15 hour-long idle lease, the 45-minute deadlock) persists while the operator believes correction is enabled. Either the shipped mode names must be `off|advise|act` as the note requires, or the note's vocabulary must be the one implemented; as committed they disagree on the one setting that decides whether the ladder acts at all.

chunk_findings.detail: `health_lines` unconditionally discards every CRASHED finding and every finding whose `evidence["via"] == "cycle"` (i.e. the LOCKED findings derived from the `cycles` argument it is handed), on the stated assumption that they are "already shown elsewhere". That assumption holds only on the `wait_order`/doctor path, where the cycle edges are emitted by `AOS.lines(ordered)`. On the `overview.py` path there is no compensating display: `overview.py` calls `health_lines(log, st, cfg, repo, wait_cycles(st, cfg))` as the sole producer of `data["health"]`, and never feeds those cycles into `AOS.lines` or any LOCKED line. Concrete failure: take the three-lane crossing-glob case the intent calls out (A waits on B, B on C, C on A); `wait_cycles(st, cfg)` yields the cycle, `HW.inspect` returns a LOCKED finding tagged `via="cycle"`, the comprehension on line 59 drops it, so `data["health"]` (and the serialized `"health": health` in the same function, and hence the brief/statusline one-liners) reports no health problem at all for a 45-minute deadlock — only the raw per-wait rows under `"waiting"` remain, which is the by-hand reading the watchdog was meant to replace. The same drop hits the fast CRASHED signal: a lane whose pid/session is gone but whose lease has not yet reached the 30-minute TTL produces a CRASHED finding that this filter removes, so none of the status/brief/doctor `health` lines show it and the crash is only noticed after the lease lapses into `recoverable` — exactly the delay the pid-in-heartbeat detector exists to avoid. The inline comment in `overview.py` even advertises "stalled / locked / runaway lanes", but the filter guarantees "locked" (and "crashed") can never appear there.

chunk_findings.detail: The knob's doc defines STALLED progress as "an event on its item other than lease bookkeeping, a commit, **an uncommitted change in its worktree**", whereas the intent defines progress as the DX-lease-progress-breakable watermark: "the last event that is not a lease renewal, plus commits in its worktree **and test jobs in flight**". Given an agent that writes edits at T0 and then hangs at T1 (the exact 2026-10-15 "agent sat idle for an hour with a current lease" case), "an uncommitted change" is *present* on every later poll, so if the detector treats that state as progress the lane is never STALLED and the watchdog's core case is missed; conversely, a lane that is genuinely alive running a long test job (the intent explicitly counts in-flight jobs as progress) is not covered by this definition and can be reported STALLED. The two definitions must match the specified watermark.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/health.py `stall_s` (progress definition)

chunk_findings.detail: The watchdog section declares only `mode`, `stall_s`, `runaway_s`, `interval_s` and `shown`. The intent requires per-lane windows for IDLE-HEARTBEAT, UNRESPONSIVE and CRASHED and names them (`[watch].idle_s`, `[watch].reply_s`, `[watch].crash_s`; the required regression test is "a dead pid is CRASHED within [watch].crash_s"), and CONFORMANCE requires "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt" (r-everything-configurable). With no `crash_s` key, an operator cannot make a dead pid/session be flagged faster than the 30-minute lease TTL ("so a dead process is seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL"); with no `idle_s`/`reply_s`, the idle-heartbeat and unanswered-nudge detectors can only run on hardcoded constants, which the conformance item forbids.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/health.py:12-42 (HealthConfig fields)

chunk_findings.detail: `mode` is a single global enum (`off | propose | apply`) applied to every finding kind, but the intent specifies the ladder "as a mode per step ([watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise, **per finding kind**)". An operator who wants to act on LOCKED (let the watchdog add the auto-order `needs` edges that end a lease deadlock) while merely reporting STALLED lanes cannot express that: `mode = "apply"` makes the pass break a stalled lane's lease and expire a crashed lane's lease as well, and `mode = "propose"` means deadlocks are never corrected. The per-finding-kind modes are not representable, so r-everything-configurable is not met for the action policy.

chunk_findings.detail:
The correction command built for a stalled lane that others are waiting on names the wrong lane. `_stalled` is passed `waiters = sorted(set(waiting_for.get(ln.item, [])))`, and in `inspect` `waiting_for` is populated as `waiting_for.setdefault(blocker, []).append(w.item)` — i.e. the values are the items of the lanes that are *blocked by* this stalled lane, not the stalled lane's own item. The fix string then does ``f"`ddflow claim {waiters[0]} --break` (its work is kept), or ask {lane.holder} to yield"``, so it claims a waiting lane's item instead of the stalled lane's item (`lane.item`) whose lease is what actually has to be freed for the waiters to proceed.

Concrete input: a stalled lane `Lane(item="A", holder="agA", live=True, progress_at=now-7200)` plus `Wait(item="B", agent="agB", on=(("A", "agA"),))`. `waiting_for["A"] == ["B"]`, so the emitted finding is ``STALLED A (agA): lease is current but no progress for 2h 0m; B waits for its files. Fix: `ddflow claim B --break` (its work is kept), or ask agA to yield``. Following that command claims/breaks B's (the waiter's) lease, which does not release A's lease, so the wait is not cleared, and it acts on the wrong lane; the target should be A (`lane.item`), whose lease is the one holding the waiters up. This matters directly for the `act` rung of the ladder, which turns `fix` into a correction ("take over … the worktree", DX-dispatch-supervise), and it contradicts the change's own requirement that a correction target the stalled holder and keep *its* work.

chunk_findings.detail: `recorded = not lz.live(lz.renewed_at)` is a tautology: it asks the lease object whether it was alive at its own `renewed_at` timestamp, and a lease whose renewal timestamp exists is by construction alive at that instant (any positive `ttl`/`grace` in `live(now, grace)` compares `now` against `renewed_at + ttl + grace`, and `renewed_at < renewed_at + ttl + grace`). So for every lane — live or dead — `recorded` is `False`, and the comment ("an expiry is recorded, whatever the clock says") is never realized. The ledger record that actually answers the question is computed nine lines above but never used for it: `recs` (line 74-76, `L.scan(...) if r.kind == "expired_lease"`) is consulted only to fill `work`. Concretely: given a lane whose holder pid is gone and whose expiry was already recorded by an earlier watchdog pass or by an operator (`lease.expired` present, `r.item in recs`), `H.inspect` still emits a CRASHED finding carrying `recorded=False`, and `correct` at line 160 evaluates `f.evidence.get("work") is True and not f.evidence["recorded"]` to True on every subsequent pass, so `mode="apply"` calls `L.expire` and appends a fresh `lease.expired` for the same item each time instead of skipping an already-recorded expiry. The intended value is `not live` in the dead-lane branch or membership in `recs`; as written the guard is dead code and the crash-expiry step is not idempotent.

chunk_findings.detail: The declared surface contradicts the mode vocabulary and the config key the change is specified against. The intent fixes the correction ladder as `[watch].act = off | advise | act` (default `advise`), but this command advertises `override [health].mode: off, propose or apply` and restrains the CLI flag with `choices=("off", "propose", "apply")`. Concretely: an operator following the spec runs `ddflow health --run --mode act` and argparse aborts with `argument --mode: invalid choice: 'act' (choose from 'off', 'propose', 'apply')`; and a project that sets the documented knob `[watch].act = "act"` is never consulted, because the callback forwards `mode=a.get("mode") or ""` and the command itself documents the engine's lookup key as `[health].mode`, so the documented setting is silently ignored and the pass stays in advise/propose behavior. Either the engine's accepted values are `advise`/`act` (the CLI then rejects every valid operator input), or they are `propose`/`apply` (the spec's `act`/`advise` names and `[watch]` key are dead), so the CLI and config surface cannot both satisfy the stated interface.

chunk_findings.detail: The watchdog that this diff exposes cannot do the fast crash detection the change exists for. The stated intent requires CRASHED to be derived from the holder's process/session being gone — "lease heartbeats carry pid, host and session id so a dead process is seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL" — bounded by a `[watch].crash_s` knob, and it separately lists IDLE-HEARTBEAT (`[watch].idle_s`) and UNRESPONSIVE (`[watch].reply_s`) as things the pass inspects. The implemented surface enumerated in this diff has none of them: the health section is exactly `mode`, `stall_s`, `runaway_s`, `interval_s`, `shown`, and the `ddflow_health` description defines the set of inspected conditions as only "STALLED …, LOCKED …, CRASHED (lease expired over work) and RUNAWAY …". Concretely, take a lane whose process is killed at t=0 while its lease still has TTL remaining: nothing in this contract looks at the pid/session, so the lane is not reported as CRASHED until the lease TTL lapses (the default 30 minutes referenced in the intent) — i.e. it reproduces the "found by reading event timestamps by hand" latency rather than the "minutes, not 30-minute TTL" requirement. Likewise a lane that keeps heartbeating but answers no nudge is not UNRESPONSIVE (no `reply_s`), and a lane that heartbeats with no other activity is only folded into `stall_s` (no distinct IDLE-HEARTBEAT). The correction contract is also flattened relative to the intent: `health.mode` is a single global `off | propose | apply`, whereas the intent calls for a mode per finding kind (`off | advise | act`), so an operator cannot, for example, advise on RUNAWAY while applying on LOCKED.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard is supposed to prove the watchdog has no kill/delete path, but the banned-substring list is both incomplete and partly vacuous, so it gives false assurance. The most common deletion call, `os.remove(path)`, matches none of the banned strings (`"rmtree"`, `"W.remove"`, `"unlink("` do not occur in `os.remove(`), and neither do `os.system("rm ...")`, `shutil.move`, or `signal.SIGKILL`; only `HW.__file__` and `H.__file__` are scanned even though the correction ladder (park/relaunch/expire) lives in the api/services layers. Concretely: add `os.remove(lockfile)` to `healthwatch` or `core.health` and this test still passes. Conversely the ban is too broad in the other direction — `"os.kill"` forbids the idiomatic non-destructive liveness probe `os.kill(pid, 0)` and `"subprocess"` forbids `ps`, exactly the tools the spec's CRASHED-by-dead-pid detection ("lease heartbeats carry pid, host and session id so a dead process is seen in minutes") would use, so the test can only be satisfied by a detector that never actually verifies the pid. The trailing `assert os.name` is a tautology (always truthy) and contributes nothing.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_health_watch.py::test_the_watchdog_has_no_process_kill_or_delete_path

chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated property ("not repeated across passes") is the opposite of what it asserts: two back-to-back `ddflow health --run --mode propose` passes are required to return byte-identical findings (`first == again`). The spec's regression list requires "findings are deduplicated and rate-limited"; if the watchdog suppresses a condition already reported within the rate-limit window, the second pass returns fewer findings and this test fails even though the behaviour is correct. So the required dedup/rate-limit across passes is neither tested nor detectable here; only within-pass key uniqueness is checked.

chunk_findings.detail: This diff hunks only the golden MCP-tool snapshot: the `as_agent` description is reworded from "A subagent's own name, this call only." to "Subagent name, this call only." across every tool. The snapshot is a derived artifact, so the only way it is legitimate is if the source-of-truth schema text was changed in the same change. If the schema string lives in one canonical place (a shared parameter model or constant), and that place still reads "A subagent's own name, this call only.", then regenerating `test_golden_mcp_tools` will yield the old text and this committed snapshot will not match, failing the golden test on the next run. The reworded string also drops the phrase "this call only", which was the part telling callers the value is not persisted; any prompt/docs/CLI help that quoted the old sentence is now inconsistent with the schema. Worth confirming the schema source was edited in lockstep with this snapshot and that no consumer depends on the removed clause.

chunk_findings.detail: The snapshot change deletes the `mode` input property from the `ddflow_health` MCP tool: the properties block now contains only `run` and `as_agent`, and `additionalProperties` remains `false`. Because the schema is generated from the tool definition, an MCP client can no longer pass `mode` to override `[health].mode` for a call — the call will be rejected (or silently ignored) as an unknown property. The stated conformance requirement is that "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt" [r-everything-configurable]; after this change the watchdog mode is settable by file/CLI/prompt but *not* by MCP, so a remote/headless MCP caller has no way to escalate a one-off `run=true` pass to `apply` (or downgrade it to `off`) even though the retained description still advertises that `run=true` "corrects per [health].mode". The concurrent rewrite of the description to "Watchdog: stalled, locked, crashed, runaway lanes and their fixes; run=true corrects per [health].mode." removes the documented `off | propose | apply` values but keeps the `mode`-driven behavior the caller can no longer control via this surface.

chunk_findings.detail: The regenerated golden usage string adds only `health` to the top-level subparser choices (`...,precommit,lanes,health,docs,metrics,...`) and still contains no `watch` entry, before or after. This usage line is the exhaustive list of top-level subcommands argparse prints, so it is direct evidence about the CLI surface the change actually ships. The intent for this change mandates a CLI surface `ddflow watch inspect|status|history|ack` (part 4, SURFACES). With the shipped parser, `ddflow watch inspect` resolves to `watch` not in the choices list, so argparse emits `ddflow: error: unrecognized arguments: watch` — the mandated inspect/status/history/ack surface does not exist. If instead the change does register a `watch` subparser elsewhere, then this golden snapshot is stale and the assertion in this transcript test fails on the new parser, because the printed choices would then include `watch` and the recorded string would not match. Either branch is a defect: the watchdog's CLI entry point is either unregistered (missing surface) or this expected-output fixture was not updated for it, while an unrelated `health` command was inserted in its place. Given input `ddflow watch inspect` (or any `watch` subcommand) the observed behavior is `unrecognized arguments`, not the specified inspection output.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent requires every limit and interval to be a knob ("every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt, per project and org"), and names `[watch].idle_s` (IDLE-HEARTBEAT), `[watch].crash_s` (CRASHED — "a dead pid is CRASHED within [watch].crash_s") and `[watch].reply_s` (UNRESPONSIVE) as such knobs, with the regression tests "a dead pid is CRASHED within [watch].crash_s". The settings dump in this transcript is the complete effective-config surface (it lists every table with its layer, including machine-explicit ones like `agent.id = 'tx' [explicit]`), and the only watch limits it contains are `health.stall_s`, `health.runaway_s`, `health.interval_s` and `health.shown`. No `health.idle_s`, `health.crash_s` or `health.reply_s` exists, and `health.mode = 'apply'` only "records a crashed lane's lease as expired" — crash detection therefore still rides the lease TTL (`lease.ttl_s = 1800`), which is the exact 30-minute delay the intent says heartbeats carrying pid/host/session id were added to eliminate. Given the motivating input — a holder whose pid is dead but whose lease was renewed moments ago — there is no knob to make that surface as CRASHED in minutes, and no way for a project or org to tune the idle-heartbeat or reply windows at all.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent specifies the correction ladder with "a mode per step ([watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise, per finding kind)". The transcript documents a single global `health.mode` (`off` | `propose` | `apply`) with one value for every lane and every finding kind. A project that wants to keep STALLED/IDLE findings advisory (report the exact command, touch nothing) while letting the watchdog actually add the auto-order `needs` edges that end a LOCKED deadlock, or record a CRASHED lane's lease expired, cannot express that: raising the knob to `apply` for the deadlock case also authorises breaking a stalled lease another agent waits for, and lowering it to `propose` disables the deadlock edges too. Because the knob is not per-kind (and, at `off`, it "inspects nothing in the periodic pass" rather than inspecting-without-acting), the ladder's step-by-step escalation the intent asks for — and the regression test "the ladder escalates step by step" — has no configuration to drive it.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change teaches the config validator's user-facing error text that the new watchdog section is called `health`, but the change's own specification defines every watchdog knob under a `[watch]` section — `[watch].stall_s`, `[watch].idle_s`, `[watch].reply_s`, `[watch].crash_s`, `[watch].interval_s`, `[watch].act` — and the CONFORMANCE clause requires "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt". The known-sections list in these two lines contains `... gates, health, ids, ...` and no `watch` anywhere (alphabetically it would sit between `upgrade` and `worktree`). Demonstrated input: an operator who follows the documented keys writes

    [watch]
    stall_s = 300
    act = "advise"

and ddflow rejects it with exactly the message these transcript lines encode — "unknown config section [watch]. Known sections: agent, bugs, …, health, …, worktree" — so the watchdog's limits/modes are not settable under the names the spec defines, and the "everything configurable" requirement is not met for this feature. Either the section must be exposed as `watch` (and this golden string must list it) or the spec's knob names must be reconciled; a test transcript whose expectation was edited to match "health" makes the mismatch self-consistent rather than fixing it.

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the top-level guard `if mode not in HW.MODES: return O.failed(...)` with a check over the *effective per-kind* modes (`bad = sorted({m for m in by_kind.values() if m not in HW.MODES})`). Because `HW.modes(cfg, mode)` is what fills `by_kind` (and the surrounding code shows it does no validation of its own — otherwise the new `bad` check would be unnecessary), the caller-supplied `mode` override is only reachable through kinds whose config is `"inherit"`. If every `[health].mode_<kind>` knob is set explicitly (e.g. `health.mode_stalled="apply"`, `health.mode_idle="apply"`, `health.mode_unresponsive="apply"`, `health.mode_locked="apply"`, `health.mode_crashed="apply"`, `health.mode_runaway="apply"`), then `by_kind` is entirely built from config, `bad` is empty, and an invalid mode passes through untouched: `ddflow health inspect --mode bogus` (also reachable via the MCP/prompt surfaces) no longer fails with `unknown mode 'bogus'`. Execution then continues with `mode` still `"bogus"`, so the outcome reports `mode:"bogus"` and `HW.record_run(log, "bogus", ...)` writes the watchdog run event with a mode value that is not one of `HW.MODES`, while the actual corrections were driven by the per-kind values. The previous code rejected this input unconditionally; validating `by_kind` instead of the resolved `mode` (or validating both) is needed to keep the guard.

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the single global gate (`cfg.health.mode == "off"`) with `all(m == "off" for m in HW.modes(cfg).values())`, i.e. the function now runs whenever *at least one* finding kind is not off. That is only correct if the findings themselves are filtered by their kind's mode somewhere, and nothing in this change does that: the only mode-aware logic added here is the short-circuit, and the `found = [...]` list that follows is produced unconditionally from `cycles`/`activity`. So with the documented per-kind knob in its own docstring (`"off" inspects nothing in the periodic pass`): set `[health] mode_idle = "off"` while the other kinds keep their `propose` default, and `all(m == "off" ...)` is False, so `health_lines` no longer returns `[]` and idle/unresponsive/locked lines for the kind the operator switched off are still emitted (and, if the same resolved mode map drives the ladder, still acted on) whenever any other kind is enabled. The input that demonstrates it is an operator config that turns off exactly one kind (`mode_locked = "off"` or `mode_idle = "off"` with the rest at the default `propose`): the gate at line 53 evaluates to False and health output for the disabled kind is produced, contradicting the contract the same diff writes into `HealthConfig.mode` ("`off` inspects nothing in the periodic pass", "mode_idle, mode_stalled, ... override it for one kind"). A per-kind-aware pass needs the per-finding kind check (skip f when `HW.modes(cfg)[f.kind] == "off"`), not just an all-off early exit.

chunk_findings.detail: The added block defines a per-finding-kind mode for six of the seven finding kinds the change is specified around: idle, stalled, unresponsive, locked, crashed, runaway — but not for STARVED. The intent enumerates STARVED as a first-class finding kind ("STARVED = context or quota pressure from the governor (P-governor sampling) so the lane cannot continue ... every found condition is a finding with evidence") and requires the correction ladder to be configurable "as a ladder with a mode per step ([watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise, per finding kind)", with the conformance requirement that "every limit, mode and interval a knob ... per project and org". Concretely: an operator whose governor starts flagging starved lanes sets `[health].mode_starved = "off"` (or `"propose"`) to handle that kind independently; no such knob is registered, so the per-kind setting cannot resolve and the generic `[health].mode` continues to govern starved findings along with everything else — exactly the coupling the per-kind knobs exist to break. The other six kinds each get their own knob, so this is an omission in the new block rather than a deliberate grouping.

chunk_findings.detail: `_unresponsive` decides UNRESPONSIVE purely from `now - lane.asked_at`, yet the condition it implements (and the text it emits, "asked … ago, no progress and no release since") requires knowing the lane produced **no progress after the ask**. The helper is handed only `lane`, `waiters` and `now` — no progress watermark (or any other "the ask was answered" signal) — so it cannot separate a lane that ignored the nudge from one that answered it by resuming work while keeping its lease. Concretely: lane L is nudged at T (because it was idle); L commits at T+5s and keeps working; at `now = T + reply_s` the watchdog calls `_unresponsive(L, [], now)`, gets `age = reply_s`, and reports "no progress and no release since" — a false statement. In `act` mode that finding feeds the ladder (the fix string itself says `park {lane.holder}'s lane`), so the watchdog parks a lane that is actively producing work, which breaks the stated invariant "never acts on a lane with progress" / "never discards work". If the intent is that `inspect()` only calls this helper for lanes whose watermark is still `<= asked_at`, that check has to exist somewhere and is not derivable from the data this function receives; as written the "no progress since" claim is unverified. (Secondary: `asked_at` is documented "0.0 for none", and `now - 0.0` gives a ~1.7e9-second age rather than "no ask", so any call for a never-nudged lane yields "asked 56 years ago" instead of being suppressed.)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new "dead process" branch is gated on `ln.work is not False`, and it `return`s unconditionally once the outer condition holds:

```python
if ln.live and ln.gone and limits.crash_s > 0 and now - ln.renewed_at >= limits.crash_s:
    if ln.work is not False:
        out.append(_dead(ln, now))
    return
```

Per the intent, `CRASHED = the holder's process or session is gone ..., or its lease expired with work attached` — the work qualifier applies only to the expired-lease clause, not to the gone-process clause (that clause exists precisely so "a dead process is seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL"). Concrete input: lane with `live=True` (lease still within TTL, `now - renewed_at = 120`), `gone=True` (pid definitely exited), `work=False`, `limits.crash_s=60`, `limits.stall_s=300`. The outer condition is true, `ln.work is not False` is false, so nothing is appended and the function returns. Because of the early `return`, the lane is also not eligible for STALLED/IDLE/UNRESPONSIVE, and the bottom CRASHED check (`if not ln.live ...`) is skipped since `ln.live` is true — the watchdog emits **no finding at all** for a lane whose process is definitively dead. The dead holder keeps its lease until the TTL lapses (the exact "stopped agent found by hand" case the change is meant to remove), and any lane waiting on that lease stays blocked; the ladder never gets a finding for the holder, so it can never park/relaunch it. This mirrors a real reachable state: a lane whose process died after/without any recorded work item (e.g. a subagent whose work field is empty).

chunk_findings.detail:
The record files are read with `f.read_text()` and only `OSError` is caught:

```python
try:
    name = f.read_text().strip()
except OSError:
    continue
```

`Path.read_text()` decodes with the locale/UTF-8 codec, and a decoding failure raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, which is a `ValueError`, not an `OSError`, so it is not caught. The identity directory is shared state written by other processes; if a record file contains bytes that are not valid UTF-8 (e.g. a non-ASCII agent name whose write was truncated by a killed harness process, leaving an incomplete multibyte sequence), `read_text()` raises, the exception escapes `liveness`, and `inspect()` — the watchdog's per-call crash check — raises instead of reporting a finding. The crash detector then fails on every call until the bad file is removed, defeating the feature; a `errors="replace"`/`errors="ignore"` read or catching `UnicodeDecodeError` would keep it read-only and total.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/harness_identity.py:liveness

chunk_findings.detail: `asked` is produced by `steps_of(...)`, which converts the stored cadence record with `clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")` — i.e. it is a timestamp on the same (injectable / simulated) clock the spec's regression tests use ("Regression tests with fake lanes and a fake clock"). `stop_notice` then computes the elapsed time with `time.time()`, the raw wall clock, instead of the same clock that produced the record. Under the fake clock required by the spec the two are unrelated: a stop recorded "5 s ago" on the fake clock at T yields `asked == T-5`, while `time.time()` returns the real epoch R (≈1.7e9), so the age handed to `clock.fmt_age` is `R-(T-5)` and the holder is told the watchdog asked it to stop decades ago (or, if the fake clock runs ahead of wall time, a negative age). Any test that asserts the notice text, and any real invocation whose clock is simulated, gets a bogus age even though `steps_of` correctly found the stop record. The elapsed-time computation needs to come from the same `clock` abstraction (e.g. `clock.now() - asked`) that generated the record.

chunk_findings.detail:
The refactor gates STALLED (and UNRESPONSIVE) correction on `f.evidence["waiters"]`, which the old `_break` did not do (it consulted `WT.waiting_for(st, cfg, f.item, now)` directly).

- In `_stalled_move`, `if not f.evidence.get("waiters"): return None` means a STALLED finding whose evidence carries no waiters produces *no move at all* — not even the ladder's first rung (nudge/stop). Given a lane that stalls while holding a renewed lease and that no other lane is currently waiting on (exactly the operator's 2026-10-15 case: an agent idle for an hour with a live lease, and the intent's `STALLED = no progress for [watch].stall_s while its lease is renewed`), `correct(..., findings=[STALLED(item="L1", evidence={...})], mode={"stalled": "apply"})` iterates the finding, `_stalled_move` hits line `if not f.evidence.get("waiters"): return None`, and returns `[]` — no nudge, no stop, no park, so the watchdog's core purpose is not served.
- The handoff is also a dead end: when a stop *was* requested and `now - asked >= cfg.health.reply_s`, `_stalled_move` returns `None` with the comment "the UNRESPONSIVE finding takes it from here", but the only UNRESPONSIVE handler in `correct` is `elif f.kind == H.UNRESPONSIVE and f.evidence.get("waiters"):`. UNRESPONSIVE is defined as "a nudge or yield request went unanswered" (evidence about the outstanding request, not about a wait-for edge), so if that finding's evidence has no `waiters` key the branch is skipped and the blocked, stalled lane is never parked/broken (its lease keeps being renewed) — the ladder silently halts after the stop request, contradicting the intent's requirement that the ladder escalates step by step (nudge → … → park → take over/relaunch) for STALLED/UNRESPONSIVE.

The `waiters` key is only needed by `_park_break` (which already re-derives claimants via `WT.waiting_for` and returns `None` if there are none); gating the earlier rungs and the UNRESPONSIVE kind on it turns several findings into no-ops.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/healthwatch.py:_stalled_move / correct (H.UNRESPONSIVE branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes the direct `h.mode == "off"` guard and replaces it with `all(m == "off" for m in modes(ctx.cfg).values())`. If `modes()` enumerates the per-kind `mode_<kind>` overrides (which is the shape its name and the newly advertised `mode_<kind>` knobs suggest) rather than resolving every kind against the global `[health].mode`, then with the default config — `[health] mode = "propose"` (or `"apply"`) and no `mode_<kind>` keys set — `modes(ctx.cfg)` is the empty mapping, `all(...)` over an empty iterable is vacuously `True`, and `cadence()` returns `[]`. The periodic watchdog pass is then never due even though the operator has the feature enabled, so no lane can ever be detected. The guard must retain the global mode, e.g. only suppress when `h.mode == "off"` *and* every explicit override is `"off"`. The input that demonstrates it is a repo with a single live lease and `[health] mode = "propose"`, `interval_s = 60`, no `mode_*` entries: the pass reads as not-due forever.

chunk_findings.detail: The watchdog spec enumerates the finding kinds as STALLED, IDLE-HEARTBEAT, LOCKED, CRASHED, RUNAWAY, UNRESPONSIVE and STARVED, and requires "a mode per step … per finding kind" with "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt" (r-everything-configurable). This diff adds a `mode_*` knob for every one of those kinds except STARVED: `mode_crashed`, `mode_idle`, `mode_locked`, `mode_runaway`, `mode_stalled`, `mode_unresponsive` are present, and the alphabetical sequence `stalled` → `unresponsive` leaves exactly the slot where `mode_starved` would sit. The remaining `mode_*` entries all carry the identical `inherit`/`health.mode` boilerplate, so the omission is not a deliberate different treatment — as written, a starved-lane finding (governor context/quota pressure, P-governor.sampling) has no per-kind mode to read: `health.mode_starved` resolves to nothing, so an operator cannot set it to `off`, nor override the inherited `health.mode` for that kind as they can for the other six. If the knob exists in another slice of this change this finding is moot; within the change as presented it is absent.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff drops the `mode` property from the `ddflow_health` input schema while leaving `"additionalProperties": false`. The intent for this change explicitly specifies that the correction ladder carries "a mode per step ([watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise, per finding kind)" and that the CONFORMANCE clause (r-everything-configurable) requires that "every limit, mode and interval a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt, per project and org". After this change an MCP client that previously issued `ddflow_health` with `{"run": true, "mode": "apply"}` (the old schema advertised `mode` = "off, propose or apply") is now rejected outright, because `mode` is no longer a declared property and `additionalProperties` is `false`. So the per-call mode override is no longer reachable over MCP even though the tool still advertises "run=true corrects per [health].mode and the mode_<kind> overrides" — the MCP surface has silently lost one of the configuration knobs the change's own conformance requirement says must be settable from every surface. If the intent was that mode is now only settable through project config, that needs to be deliberate (and MCP/CLI/prompt parity verified), not achieved by deleting the parameter from the schema.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten `health.stall_s` help text is internally contradictory and, taken literally, describes a progress rule that would suppress the very STALLED findings the watchdog exists for. It says a lane counts as showing progress if there was "a change in its worktree since the lease began", and then, in the same paragraph, says "neither is a file that was changed once and never again" progress. Those two statements cannot both hold: a file changed once after the lease began *is* a change "since the lease began" (so, per the parenthetical, it is progress and the lane is never STALLED), while the closing sentence says exactly that case is *not* progress. Concrete input: a lane takes a lease at T, writes one file at T+300s and then does nothing but renew its heartbeat; at T+stall_s (default 3600s) the parenthetical ("change since the lease began") marks it as progressing, so it is never reported STALLED — which is precisely the 2026-10-15 failure mode ("an agent sat idle for an hour with a current lease (a heartbeat loop kept renewing it)") the watchdog is supposed to catch. Only the closing sentence (a one-off change is not progress) yields the intended behaviour, so the parenthetical must be scoped to the current stall window (a change since the last inspection / since the progress watermark), not "since the lease began". As written, the operator-facing help documents a rule under which a stalled lane with any historical worktree write is never flagged.

chunk_findings.detail: The recorded intent for this watchdog fixes the mode vocabulary: "mode off|advise|act" (with default advise), and the governing note that renames the CLI (`ddflow watch …` → `ddflow health …`) explicitly says only the CLI name changes — "The ladder stays: nudge -> ask status -> request yield -> park -> take over/relaunch -> escalate, mode off|advise|act." The help text added here instead advertises the per-kind knobs as taking `'off'`, `'propose'` or `'apply'` (e.g. `health.mode_idle`, `health.mode_stalled`, `health.mode_unresponsive`, `health.mode_locked`, `health.mode_crashed`, `health.mode_runaway`), i.e. a different vocabulary from the one the operator/roadmap specified. Concrete failure: an operator who follows the documented ladder and sets `health.mode = act` (or per-kind `health.mode_stalled = act`) hits the "unrecognised value" path described in the very same help text — a warning plus a silent fall back to `'propose'` — so the watchdog stays in report-only mode and never performs the stop/park/relaunch steps the operator asked for, with no error surfaced beyond a warning.

chunk_findings.detail: The old test ran the watchdog twice in `--mode propose` and asserted that the two findings lists were element-wise identical and that `(kind, item, holder)` keys were unique; the new test only runs one propose pass and checks `len(keys) == len(set(keys))` for that single pass. Findings are recomputed on every pass, so the requirement that findings are not duplicated/accumulated *across passes* is now untested: an implementation that persists findings and re-appends them (or otherwise returns pass-1 findings plus new ones on pass 2) would still satisfy `keys == set(keys)` on the single `first` pass, would still write exactly one `health_stop:T1` if the request dedup is based on the pending reply window rather than on the finding list, and would still return one non-applied "waiting" move on the 4th apply — so the new test passes while the removed one failed. Since the stated regression set explicitly requires "findings are deduplicated and rate-limited", dropping the only cross-pass check for this is a coverage regression in the change's own test file.

chunk_findings.detail: The test encodes a CRASHED definition that is narrower than the one the watchdog is specified to implement. The intent defines CRASHED as "the holder's process or session is gone (lease heartbeats carry pid, host and session id so a dead process is seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL), **or** its lease expired with work attached". The "with work attached" qualifier attaches only to the *expired-lease* branch; the dead-process branch has no work condition. The test, however, builds `clean = H.Lane("T1", A, True, NOW - 30, work=False, renewed_at=NOW - 90, gone=True)` — a leader whose lease is still live (renewed 90 s ago, 30‑minute TTL not reached) and whose process/session is gone (`gone=True`) — and asserts `H.inspect([clean], [], [], [], NOW, LIM2) == []`, i.e. that no finding is produced because there is "nothing to lose". Given that input the spec requires a CRASHED finding within `crash_s` (60 s here, and `renewed_at` is already 90 s stale). As written, a dead lease holder with a clean worktree is silently ignored until the lease TTL lapses — up to 30 minutes — even though it still holds the task/lease and its dispatcher slot, which is exactly the failure mode ("seen in minutes, not after the 30-minute TTL") the feature exists to prevent. The sibling integration test `test_a_dead_harness_...` only exercises the `work=True`/file-written case, so nothing else in this diff catches the gated behavior.

chunk_findings.detail: The `declare` carve-out is keyed on the bare *enclosing function name* and is applied to **all six** `WATCHDOG` modules and to **every** `_deletes()` call inside that function, not just the identity-record write the comment names. Demonstration: add to `services/healthwatch.py` a method `def declare(self, lane): shutil.rmtree(lane.worktree)` (or `os.remove(lease_path)`, `lane_tree.rename(...)`). `_calls()` reports `fn == "declare"`, so the guard at line 98 evaluates `fn != "declare"` as False and skips the call; `test_the_watchdog_modules_signal_nothing_and_delete_nothing` passes while the watchdog has just destroyed a lane's work. This directly contradicts the module docstring's stated invariant that "The watchdog's own modules additionally may not delete anything at all," and the hole is not even scoped to `surfaces/declared/health.py` — any of the six listed modules may host a `declare` function and thereby gain an undetected delete/move/replace.

chunk_findings.detail: Detection keys on the literal call name (`f.attr` / `getattr(f, "id", "")`), so a trivially aliased import evades both `test_every_process_signal_in_ddflow_is_on_a_child_it_started` and the watchdog check. Input: `from os import killpg as _kp` followed by `_kp(pgid, signal.SIGKILL)` yields `name == "_kp"`, which is not in `KILLERS` and not handled by `_is_probe`, so no `unlisted`/`bad` entry is produced; likewise `getattr(os, "kill")(pid, signal.SIGKILL)` yields `name == "getattr"`. The docstring's claim that "every call that can end a process ... must be one of the sites below" is therefore unenforced against exactly the kind of accidental kill (signalling a pid ddflow did not start) the file exists to forbid.

chunk_findings.detail: The watchdog ladder the change is implementing is recorded as `[watch].act = off | advise | act, default advise` (intent §3), and the ROADMAP note only rebrands the CLI verbs (`ddflow watch inspect|…` → `ddflow health inspect|…`) — it does not rename the ladder knob or change its mode set/default. The transcript the change adds, however, fixes the watchdog's correcting mode as `health.mode = 'propose'` and then makes every per-kind setting (`health.mode_idle/stalled/locked/crashed/runaway/unresponsive = 'inherit'`) resolve to it. `'propose'` is not a member of the recorded `off | advise | act` set, and `advise` — the documented default — does not appear anywhere in the new block. Concretely: an operator who reads the documented ladder and runs with the documented default (mode `advise`, i.e. "write findings only, change nothing") gets the `propose` mode instead, and a config validated against the recorded enum (`off|advise|act`) would reject the fixture's default outright. If the intent is that `advise` was renamed, the golden transcript should record the recorded value; if not, the fixture enshrines a mode that violates the ladder contract.

chunk_findings.detail: Intent §1 enumerates seven findings that the watchdog must produce: STALLED, IDLE-HEARTBEAT, LOCKED, CRASHED, RUNAWAY, UNRESPONSIVE and STARVED (governor context/quota pressure, P-governor sampling), and §3 says the correcting mode is set "per finding kind" with the CONFORMANCE clause `r-everything-configurable` requiring every mode to be a knob. The new block supplies per-kind mode knobs for exactly six kinds (`mode_idle`, `mode_stalled`, `mode_unresponsive`, `mode_locked`, `mode_crashed`, `mode_runaway`) and none for STARVED. Given a lane that is STARVED by governor quota pressure, no per-kind mode can be set for it (it can only fall back to the base `health.mode`), so the per-finding-kind configurability the spec demands is absent for one of the enumerated kinds — and the golden transcript locks that gap in.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `[health].mode` doc states that `apply` "adds the auto-order `needs` edges that end a lease deadlock (this mode decides for the pass, whatever `[schedule].auto_order` says)", while the `schedule.auto_order` knob documented in this same surface says of `off`: "does nothing", and promises ddflow "never touches a done, abandoned or decide item, an item tagged no-auto-order, or adds an edge that would close a needs cycle". Two knobs therefore govern the same action and one silently overrides the other's explicit `off`. Input that demonstrates it: `[schedule] auto_order = "off"` (operator has switched off silent auto-rewiring) together with `[health] mode = "apply"`; a three-lane crossing-glob deadlock arrives, and the watchdog adds the `needs` edges anyway — the one action `auto_order = "off"` says will never happen. Nothing in the `health.mode` text commits the watchdog to the other two guards either, so an item tagged `no-auto-order` can be rewired, and an edge that closes a `needs` cycle can be added, after which the default `schedule.cycle_policy = "error"` refuses to schedule the queue at all. Either `auto_order`'s "does nothing" contract or the "whatever `[schedule].auto_order` says" override is wrong as written.

chunk_findings.detail: The governing note for this change fixes the watchdog's mode vocabulary as `off | advise | act` ("The ladder stays: nudge -> ask status -> request yield -> park -> take over/relaunch -> escalate, mode off|advise|act"), but the config text this diff commits documents `health.mode = 'propose'` and accepts only `'off'`, `'propose'`, `'apply'` (`health.mode_idle/stalled/unresponsive/locked/crashed/runaway` likewise). Concretely, an operator following the recorded vocabulary sets `ddflow config --set health.mode act` (or `advise`) to turn the correction ladder on; `act` is not a recognised value, so per the very text committed here the knob is "warned about, reported by `doctor` and falls back to 'propose'" — i.e. report-only. The watchdog then nudges nothing, parks nothing and breaks no lease, so the stall the change exists to correct (the 2026-10-15 hour-long idle lease, the 45-minute deadlock) persists while the operator believes correction is enabled. Either the shipped mode names must be `off|advise|act` as the note requires, or the note's vocabulary must be the one implemented; as committed they disagree on the one setting that decides whether the ladder acts at all.

The updated known-sections list now contains `health` but still (and now deliberately) omits `watch`, so the config section names the watchdog spec actually uses are not registered anywhere. The intent and its CONFORMANCE clause define every limit, mode and interval as a knob named `[watch].stall_s`, `[watch].idle_s`, `[watch].reply_s`, `[watch].interval_s`, `[watch].crash_s`, `[watch].act`; the ROADMAP note only remaps the CLI verbs (`ddflow watch inspect|status|history|ack` → `ddflow health …`) and says nothing about renaming the config section. Concretely: an operator who follows the spec and writes

    [watch]
    stall_s = 300

into project config, or runs `ddflow config set watch.stall_s 300`, still gets the string shown on this line, `unknown config section [watch]. Known sections: agent, … gates, health, hooks, …`, and the edit is rejected — while `[health]` is accepted. Either the registry should accept the spec'd `[watch]` keys, or the intent's knob names must be renamed to `[health].*`; as it stands no watchdog limit, mode or interval is settable under the documented name, breaking the "everything configurable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt" conformance requirement, and there is no `watch` entry between `upgrade` and `worktree` in this list to fall back on.
